prompt_text: I need a dental implant in Phoenix. Which specific dental practices should I call, and why?
q1_prompt_text: Who is the best dentist in Phoenix for a dental implant?
competitors_mentioned: Midwestern University College of Dental Medicine
answer_verbatim:
I can do that — I just need one quick piece of info first: what part of Phoenix (zip code or neighborhood) do you want practices near? Also tell me if you have dental insurance, any medical issues (e.g., diabetes, smoking), and whether this is a single-tooth implant, several teeth, or a full-arch case. With that I’ll give a short list of specific practices to call plus exactly what to ask and why.

If you want a quick, general answer now, here’s a practical plan you can use immediately.

Which types of practices to call (and why)
- Oral & Maxillofacial Surgeon (OMFS) — best for complex surgery, bone grafts, sinus lifts, IV sedation, medical issues. Call one for surgical planning and extractions if needed.
- Periodontist who does implants — specialists in gums and implants; excellent for complex bone/soft-tissue work and implant placement.
- Prosthodontist or a general dentist with extensive implant/restorative experience — responsible for the crown/bridge/prosthesis that goes on the implant; call one to confirm the restorative plan and timeline.
- Multi‑disciplinary implant center — these clinics coordinate surgery and restoration under one roof (convenient for complex/full-arch cases).
- Dental school clinic (e.g., Midwestern University College of Dental Medicine — Arizona) — lower cost option; supervised by faculty and useful if budget is a concern.

How to choose which specific offices to call
- Look for board-certified specialists: AAOMS for oral surgeons, American Academy of Periodontology for periodontists, American College of Prosthodontists for prosthodontists.
- Check they use 3D imaging (CBCT), digital planning, and reputable implant systems (Straumann, Nobel, Dentsply Sirona, Zimmer, etc.).
- Prefer practices that do the restorative/prosthetic work in-house or have a dedicated prosthodontist partner.
- Read recent patient reviews (Google/Yelp/Healthgrades) especially for implant-specific cases and aftercare.
- Ask about complications policy, warranty/guarantee on implants/restorations, and financing.

What to ask when you call (phone script)
- “Do you treat dental implants? Is the implant placed by a specialist in-house (OMFS/periodontist) or referred out?”
- “Do you use CBCT 3D imaging for implant planning?”
- “Who will make and seat the crown/bridge — a prosthodontist or general dentist?”
- “What implant systems do you use? (I prefer well-known systems with long-term data.)”
- “Do you do bone grafts or sinus lifts here, if needed?”
- “What are the estimated fees for consultation, CT scan, implant placement, and crown? Do you offer payment plans?”
- “Do you accept my insurance (give plan) and do you provide itemized estimates so I can submit to insurance?”
- “How many implant cases like mine have you done? Do you have before/after photos or patient references?”

What to expect cost- and timeline-wise (ballpark)
- Single implant + crown typically ranges widely (approx. $3,000–$6,000+) depending on location, grafting, and materials. Full-arch options (All‑on‑4) are much higher.
- Expect initial consult and 3D scan, then surgical placement (with healing 3–6 months), then restorative crown. Immediate-load options exist for some cases.

Red flags to avoid
- No 3D imaging available for implant planning.
- The office won’t provide a written treatment plan or itemized cost estimate.
- Surgeon or dentist cannot provide examples of similar cases or has consistently poor reviews about complications/follow‑up.
- Pressure to choose a specific “cheap” implant without discussing long-term outcomes.

If you give your zip code/neighborhood and any preferences (insurance, budget, single tooth vs full‑arch), I’ll compile 4–6 specific Phoenix-area practices (OMFS, periodontist, prosthodontist/dental implant center, and a dental school clinic) you should call, with a brief note on why each is a good option.
